# Search Studio

> Free, open-source visual studio for AI search algorithms: BFS, DFS, DFID, A*, IDA*, hill climbing, simulated annealing, genetic algorithms, ant colony, TSP heuristics, Minimax, Alpha-Beta, SSS*, planning, AO*, Rete and constraint satisfaction. Step-by-step OPEN/CLOSED traces, beginner explanations and printable exports.

Search Studio is a free, public-domain web app (made by 1mystic, https://github.com/1mystic) that accompanies the course "AI: Search Methods for Problem Solving" (NPTEL / IIT Madras, Prof. Deepak Khemani). It is an independent study aid. Every algorithm has a static explanation page and an interactive step-by-step trace at https://1mystic.github.io/SearchStudio/#try-<id>.

Conventions used in every trace: OPEN and CLOSED hold node pairs (node, parent, depth or g); ties break alphabetically; the goal test happens when a node is picked from OPEN; simulated annealing accepts a worse move with probability 1/(1+e^(-ΔE/T)); savings are S(i,j) = C(b,i) + C(b,j) − C(i,j).

## Week 2

- [Breadth First Search](https://1mystic.github.io/SearchStudio/learn/search-bfs.html): OPEN is a queue: new children are appended, so the shallowest node is expanded first. Finds a path with the fewest edges.
- [Depth First Search](https://1mystic.github.io/SearchStudio/learn/search-dfs.html): OPEN is a stack: new children are prepended, so the deepest node is expanded first. Little memory, no optimality.
- [Depth-Bounded DFS](https://1mystic.github.io/SearchStudio/learn/search-dfs-bounded.html): Depth First Search that refuses to generate children below a depth bound. Memory stays small and loops cannot run away, but a goal deeper than the bound is missed.
- [Depth First Iterative Deepening](https://1mystic.github.io/SearchStudio/learn/search-dfid.html): Run depth-bounded DFS with bound 0, 1, 2, … until the goal is found. The path of BFS with the memory of DFS, at the price of repeated work.
- [BFS on a state space](https://1mystic.github.io/SearchStudio/learn/statespace-bfs.html): OPEN is a queue of node pairs (state, parent, depth). The graph is never listed: MoveGen produces each state's neighbours on demand, and only the explored part is drawn. Finds a solution with the fewest moves.
- [DFS on a state space](https://1mystic.github.io/SearchStudio/learn/statespace-dfs.html): OPEN is a stack of node pairs (state, parent, depth): the newest children are picked first, so the search dives deep before it backs up. Finds a solution, usually not the shortest.
- [Simple search (no node pairs)](https://1mystic.github.io/SearchStudio/learn/statespace-simple.html): OPEN and CLOSED hold only states. The search can say that a goal is reachable, but it cannot say how: with no parent stored, the path is lost. A demonstration of why the course keeps node pairs.

## Week 3

- [Hill climbing in the blocks world (h1 vs h2)](https://1mystic.github.io/SearchStudio/learn/plan-hill-climbing.html): Steepest-ascent hill climbing on blocks-world states. The simple heuristic h1 (+1 per block on the right thing, −1 otherwise) gets stuck at a local maximum; h2 (credit for a whole correct tower) reaches the goal.
- [Brute force (exact)](https://1mystic.github.io/SearchStudio/learn/tsp-brute-force.html): Fix the first city and try every ordering of the rest; for a symmetric TSP each tour appears twice, so (n−1)!/2 distinct tours.
- [Brute force (truth table)](https://1mystic.github.io/SearchStudio/learn/sat-brute-force.html): Try all 2ⁿ assignments in binary order and count the satisfied clauses of each. The rows with h = m are the solutions, so brute force is exact but doubles with every variable (limited to 6 variables here).
- [Nearest Neighbour](https://1mystic.github.io/SearchStudio/learn/tsp-nearest-neighbour.html): Grow one path from a start city, always moving to the closest unvisited city; return home at the end.
- [Hill climbing (N1)](https://1mystic.github.io/SearchStudio/learn/sat-hill-climbing.html): From a start assignment move to the best one-flip neighbour, but only if it satisfies strictly more clauses. It stops at a local maximum or a plateau, which may be below the solution.
- [Greedy heuristic](https://1mystic.github.io/SearchStudio/learn/tsp-greedy.html): Scan edges shortest first; accept an edge unless a city would get degree 3 or a cycle shorter than n would close.
- [Beam search](https://1mystic.github.io/SearchStudio/learn/sat-beam.html): Keep w assignments instead of one. Each level generates the N1 neighbours of every assignment in the beam and keeps the w with the largest h; stop when the head of the beam no longer improves. w = 1 is hill climbing.
- [Savings heuristic](https://1mystic.github.io/SearchStudio/learn/tsp-savings.html): Start with an out-and-back trip from the base to every city, then merge trips in decreasing order of savings S(i,j) = C(base,i) + C(base,j) − C(i,j).
- [Variable Neighbourhood Descent (N1 → N1–n)](https://1mystic.github.io/SearchStudio/learn/sat-vnd.html): Hill climb in N1. When no one-flip neighbour is better, enlarge the neighbourhood to N1–2 (one or two flips), then N1–3, and so on up to N1–n; after every improvement go back to N1.
- [2-city exchange](https://1mystic.github.io/SearchStudio/learn/tsp-two-city-exchange.html): Swap the positions of any two cities: n(n−1)/2 neighbours. Steepest-descent hill climbing until no swap helps.
- [Best First Search](https://1mystic.github.io/SearchStudio/learn/search-best-first.html): OPEN is a priority queue on h(N), the heuristic estimate of distance to the goal. Fast when h is good, not optimal.
- [Best neighbour, fixed moves](https://1mystic.github.io/SearchStudio/learn/sat-best-neighbour.html): Always move to the best one-flip neighbour, even if it is no better than the current string, for a fixed number of moves. With no memory it can walk in circles, which is the problem tabu search fixes.
- [2-edge exchange (2-opt)](https://1mystic.github.io/SearchStudio/learn/tsp-two-edge-exchange.html): Remove two non-adjacent edges and reconnect the other way, which reverses the block between them: n(n−3)/2 neighbours.
- [Hill Climbing](https://1mystic.github.io/SearchStudio/learn/search-hill-climbing.html): Move to the best-looking neighbour (lowest h) as long as it improves on the current node. Constant memory, but it stops at the first local optimum, which need not be the goal.
- [Or-opt (move a city)](https://1mystic.github.io/SearchStudio/learn/tsp-or-opt.html): Take one city out and insert it between two other neighbours: a special 3-edge exchange.
- [Beam Search](https://1mystic.github.io/SearchStudio/learn/search-beam.html): Generate the children of every node in the beam and keep only the w best by h. Memory is bounded by w; a narrow beam can discard the only way to the goal.
- [Tabu search](https://1mystic.github.io/SearchStudio/learn/sat-tabu.html): Always flip the best variable that is not tabu, even if that makes h worse. A variable just flipped is tabu for the next tt iterations; aspiration lets a tabu flip through if it beats the best h seen; an optional frequency penalty discourages variables flipped too often.
- [3-edge exchange](https://1mystic.github.io/SearchStudio/learn/tsp-three-edge-exchange.html): Remove three edges and reconnect the three segments in a new way (pure 3-opt moves).
- [Variable neighbourhood descent](https://1mystic.github.io/SearchStudio/learn/tsp-vnd.html): Hill climb with a sparse neighbourhood, then continue from its local optimum with denser ones. A local optimum of one MoveGen need not be one of the next.
- [Random walk](https://1mystic.github.io/SearchStudio/learn/sat-random-walk.html): At every step flip one randomly chosen variable and accept the result whatever its h. Remember the best string seen. It never gets stuck, but it does not use h to steer either.
- [Beam search](https://1mystic.github.io/SearchStudio/learn/tsp-beam.html): Keep the w best neighbours of all beam members at every level; stop when the best of the level is no better than the best so far. w = 1 is hill climbing.
- [Tabu search](https://1mystic.github.io/SearchStudio/learn/tsp-tabu.html): Always move to the best neighbour that is not tabu, even if it is worse. A move's key (the swapped pair / removed edges) stays tabu for tt iterations; aspiration allows a tabu move that beats bestSeen.
- [Iterated hill climbing](https://1mystic.github.io/SearchStudio/learn/tsp-ihc.html): Repeat: random start tour, steepest-descent hill climbing to a local optimum. Return the best local optimum found.
- [Best neighbour, k moves](https://1mystic.github.io/SearchStudio/learn/tsp-best-neighbour-moves.html): From the start tour, move to the best neighbour every time for a fixed number of moves, even when it is worse than the current tour. At a local optimum the best neighbour is worse, and the next best neighbour is usually the tour we just left, so the search cycles.
- [Random walk](https://1mystic.github.io/SearchStudio/learn/tsp-random-walk.html): Pure exploration: ignore the evaluation function and step to a random neighbour each time, remembering the best tour seen.
- [Simulated annealing](https://1mystic.github.io/SearchStudio/learn/tsp-sa.html): Pick a random neighbour and move to it with probability P = 1/(1 + e^(−ΔE/T)), ΔE = cost(current) − cost(next). T falls geometrically: high T ≈ coin flip, T → 0 ≈ hill climbing.
- [Best First on a state space](https://1mystic.github.io/SearchStudio/learn/statespace-best-first.html): OPEN is ordered by the heuristic h alone: the state that looks closest to the goal is expanded next. Often fast, never guaranteed to give the shortest solution.

## Week 4

- [Game of Life: generation stepper](https://1mystic.github.io/SearchStudio/learn/life-stepper.html): Every cell looks only at its eight neighbours: a dead cell with exactly 3 live neighbours is born, a live cell with 2 or 3 survives, every other live cell dies. Watch order and motion emerge from that one local rule.
- [Iterated hill climbing](https://1mystic.github.io/SearchStudio/learn/sat-ihc.html): Hill climbing gets stuck on plateaus and local maxima, so restart it from several different assignments and keep the best result. Starts can be typed in or drawn from a seeded random generator.
- [Stochastic hill climbing (fixed T)](https://1mystic.github.io/SearchStudio/learn/sat-stochastic-hc.html): Pick a random one-flip neighbour and move to it with probability P = 1/(1 + e^(−ΔE/T)), ΔE = h(new) − h(current), at a constant temperature T. Better moves are likely, worse moves are possible.
- [Simulated annealing](https://1mystic.github.io/SearchStudio/learn/sat-sa.html): Stochastic hill climbing whose temperature falls: pick a random bit flip, accept with P = 1/(1 + e^(−ΔE/T)), ΔE = h(new) − h(current), then cool. High T behaves like a random walk, T → 0 like hill climbing.
- [Genetic algorithm](https://1mystic.github.io/SearchStudio/learn/sat-ga.html): A population of bit strings. Fitness = h (clauses satisfied); roulette-wheel selection picks parents with probability h / Σh, one-point crossover builds two children per pair, and mutation flips a random bit with probability pm.
- [Stochastic hill climbing](https://1mystic.github.io/SearchStudio/learn/tsp-stochastic-hc.html): Pick a random neighbour and move to it with probability P = 1/(1 + e^(−ΔE/T)), ΔE = cost(current) − cost(next), at a fixed temperature T. The first step shows the sigmoid for several T (ΔE = 0 gives P = ½).
- [Genetic algorithm](https://1mystic.github.io/SearchStudio/learn/tsp-ga.html): Population of tours. Roulette-wheel selection (fitness = K / cost), pairwise crossover, swap mutation, then the weakest members are replaced by the strongest offspring.
- [Crossover lab](https://1mystic.github.io/SearchStudio/learn/tsp-crossover-lab.html): Apply one TSP crossover to two parents: cycle, PMX, order (path representation), alternating edges and heuristic (adjacency), ordinal + single-point, or naive single-point to see why it fails.
- [Representation lab](https://1mystic.github.io/SearchStudio/learn/tsp-representation-lab.html): Convert a tour between path, ordinal and adjacency representations step by step; see that the reversed tour's adjacency is also valid, that one-point crossover on ordinal strings always decodes to a tour, and that the same cut on adjacency lists may not.
- [Ant colony optimisation](https://1mystic.github.io/SearchStudio/learn/tsp-aco.html): Each ant builds a tour city by city with P(i→j) ∝ τ^α (1/d)^β over unvisited cities. Then pheromone evaporates, τ ← (1−ρ)τ, and every ant deposits Q/L on the edges of its tour.

## Week 5

- [Branch & bound (exact)](https://1mystic.github.io/SearchStudio/learn/tsp-branch-and-bound.html): Refine a set of tours by deciding one edge at a time: include it or exclude it. Every node gets the lower bound ½ Σ (two cheapest admissible edges at each city); a node whose bound is no better than the best tour found is pruned.
- [Uniform Cost Search](https://1mystic.github.io/SearchStudio/learn/search-ucs.html): OPEN is a priority queue on g(N), the cost so far. A cheaper path to a node on OPEN or CLOSED updates its parent. Optimal for non-negative costs.
- [Dijkstra's Algorithm](https://1mystic.github.io/SearchStudio/learn/search-dijkstra.html): Every node is WHITE (not final) or BLACK (shortest distance known). Repeatedly blacken the WHITE node with the least d and relax its edges. Stops when the goal turns BLACK.
- [Branch & Bound (state space)](https://1mystic.github.io/SearchStudio/learn/search-branch-and-bound.html): Tree search with OPEN ordered on g and no CLOSED list. The same state can appear many times in the search tree; the tracer counts the occurrences. The first goal picked is the cheapest path.
- [British Museum (brute force on paths)](https://1mystic.github.io/SearchStudio/learn/search-british-museum.html): Try every simple path from S to the goal and keep the cheapest. Always right, hopelessly slow on big graphs: the yardstick the clever algorithms are measured against.
- [A*](https://1mystic.github.io/SearchStudio/learn/search-astar.html): OPEN is a priority queue on f(N) = g(N) + w·h(N). With w = 1 and an admissible h (h ≤ h*) the first goal picked is optimal. w > 1 is weighted A*: faster, not guaranteed optimal.
- [Weighted A*](https://1mystic.github.io/SearchStudio/learn/search-weighted-astar.html): A* with f = g + w·h, w ≥ 1. Trusting h more makes the search greedier and usually faster. With an admissible h the path cost is at most w times the optimum C*.
- [Heuristic comparison (A* with h = 0, h, h*)](https://1mystic.github.io/SearchStudio/learn/search-heuristic-comparison.html): Runs A* three times: with h = 0 (which is UCS), with the problem's h, and with the perfect h = h*. Compares nodes expanded and the effective branching factor b*: a better heuristic means fewer expansions.
- [A* on a state space](https://1mystic.github.io/SearchStudio/learn/statespace-astar.html): OPEN is ordered by f = g + h. With an admissible h (tiles out of place or Manhattan, for the 8-puzzle) the first goal picked is a shortest solution; the sharper h expands fewer states.

## Week 6

- [Sequence alignment (dynamic programming)](https://1mystic.github.io/SearchStudio/learn/align-dp.html): Fill a table D(i,j) = cheapest alignment of the first i letters of a with the first j letters of b, one row at a time, then trace back the optimal path through the lattice.
- [A* with upper-bound pruning of OPEN](https://1mystic.github.io/SearchStudio/learn/search-astar-ub.html): A* that never puts a node with f > U on OPEN, where U is the cost of any known solution (here a quick greedy run, or a value you type). Those nodes cannot lie on a cheaper path when h is admissible, so OPEN stays smaller and the answer is unchanged.
- [Sequence alignment (A*)](https://1mystic.github.io/SearchStudio/learn/align-astar.html): Treat each lattice point (i,j) as a state and search from (0,0) to (m,n) with A*. h(i,j) = gap × |(m−i) − (n−j)| never overestimates, because that many gaps are unavoidable.
- [Breadth First Heuristic Search (BFHS)](https://1mystic.github.io/SearchStudio/learn/search-bfhs.html): Expand the graph layer by layer like breadth-first search, but never generate a node with f = g + h above an upper bound U. Only the boundary (the last two layers) is kept in CLOSED, older layers are deleted. With admissible h the cost equals A*'s.
- [Divide and Conquer BFHS (DC-BFHS)](https://1mystic.github.io/SearchStudio/learn/search-dc-bfhs.html): BFHS keeps only boundary layers, so it cannot read the path back. DC-BFHS remembers a relay node from the middle layer of the best path, then solves start→relay and relay→goal as two smaller BFHS problems, recursively. No parent pointers are stored at all.
- [Divide and Conquer Beam Search](https://1mystic.github.io/SearchStudio/learn/search-dc-beam.html): Beam search keeps only the w best nodes of each layer and only the latest layers, so it cannot read its path back. Divide and Conquer Beam Search remembers a relay node from the middle layer of the best path found, then solves start→relay and relay→goal as two smaller beam searches, recursively. Memory is O(w), with no parent pointers.
- [Beam Stack Search](https://1mystic.github.io/SearchStudio/learn/search-beam-stack.html): Beam search with memory of what it threw away. Each layer keeps its w best nodes by f, and a beam stack records the range of f values [lo, hi) each layer has covered. After a layer is exhausted the search backtracks to the deepest layer with unexplored f values, so it is eventually complete and optimal.
- [Smart Memory Graph Search (SMGS)](https://1mystic.github.io/SearchStudio/learn/search-smgs.html): A* that prunes CLOSED. A closed node whose neighbours have all been expanded can never be regenerated, so it is interior. Interior nodes are deleted, except relay nodes that still lie on the parent chain of a live node (OPEN or boundary), which are kept so the path can be read back.
- [Admissibility & monotone check](https://1mystic.github.io/SearchStudio/learn/search-monotone-check.html): Compute the true remaining cost h* by a backward Dijkstra from the goal, then test every node for admissibility (h ≤ h*) and every edge for the monotone condition h(m) ≤ k(m,n) + h(n).
- [Frontier Search](https://1mystic.github.io/SearchStudio/learn/search-frontier.html): A* with no CLOSED list at all. Each OPEN node remembers which of its moves lead back to nodes already expanded (used-operator bits), so the parents are never regenerated. Memory is just the frontier.
- [IDA*](https://1mystic.github.io/SearchStudio/learn/search-ida-star.html): Depth-first search that never expands a node with f = g + h above a bound. Start with bound f(S); after a failed pass, raise the bound to the smallest f that was cut off. Optimal with admissible h, memory linear in depth.
- [Recursive Best-First Search](https://1mystic.github.io/SearchStudio/learn/search-rbfs.html): Explore the best child while its f stays below the best alternative elsewhere; when it exceeds that limit, back up its f value and switch. Keeps only the current path and its siblings.
- [Divide & Conquer Frontier Search](https://1mystic.github.io/SearchStudio/learn/search-dcfs.html): Frontier search drops CLOSED: each OPEN node remembers which neighbours already used an edge to it, so expanded nodes are never regenerated. A relay node halfway along each path lets the path be rebuilt by two smaller searches.

## Week 7

- [Minimax](https://1mystic.github.io/SearchStudio/learn/game-minimax.html): Evaluate the game tree depth-first from left to right: a MAX node takes the largest child value, a MIN node the smallest. The root's value is the outcome with best play from both sides.
- [Alpha-Beta pruning](https://1mystic.github.io/SearchStudio/learn/game-alpha-beta.html): Carry a window (α, β): α is the best value MAX can already guarantee, β the best MIN can guarantee. When α ≥ β at a node, the remaining children cannot matter and are pruned.
- [SSS*](https://1mystic.github.io/SearchStudio/learn/game-sss-star.html): A best-first algorithm for game trees. OPEN holds triples (node, LIVE or SOLVED, merit h). It refines the most promising strategy first and never evaluates a leaf that Alpha-Beta would prune; it can skip leaves Alpha-Beta evaluates.
- [k-ply tic-tac-toe (static evaluator, horizon effect)](https://1mystic.github.io/SearchStudio/learn/ttt-kply.html): Look only k plies ahead, score the frontier with e(n) = (lines still open for X) − (lines still open for O), and back the values up with minimax. Then compare with a full-depth search to see what lies beyond the horizon.
- [Expectiminimax (supplementary)](https://1mystic.github.io/SearchStudio/learn/game-expectiminimax.html): Supplementary (Russell & Norvig, games of chance). Minimax for games with dice or cards: MAX takes the largest child, MIN the smallest, and a chance node takes the expected value, the sum of probability × child value. With no chance nodes it is exactly Minimax.
- [Dominant strategies and Nash equilibria (supplementary)](https://1mystic.github.io/SearchStudio/learn/game-nash.html): Supplementary. Remove strictly dominated strategies one at a time, then mark each player's best responses: a cell where both are best responses is a pure Nash equilibrium. Flags equilibria that both players would swap for something better.

## Week 8

- [Forward state-space planning](https://1mystic.github.io/SearchStudio/learn/plan-forward.html): Search forward from the initial state: every applicable operator gives a successor state. Breadth-first search returns a shortest plan, but the branching factor is the number of applicable actions.
- [Backward state-space planning](https://1mystic.github.io/SearchStudio/learn/plan-backward.html): Search backwards from the goal. An operator is relevant if it adds a goal and deletes none; regressing the goal set G through it gives (G − add) ∪ pre. Stop when the initial state satisfies the current goal set.
- [Goal Stack Planning](https://1mystic.github.io/SearchStudio/learn/plan-gsp.html): Keep a stack of goals and actions. Pop satisfied goals; replace an unsatisfied goal by an action that achieves it plus that action's preconditions; when an action reaches the top its preconditions hold, so apply it. Goals are solved one at a time, which is why the Sussman anomaly makes it undo its own work.
- [Graphplan](https://1mystic.github.io/SearchStudio/learn/plan-graphplan.html): Build a planning graph of alternating proposition and action layers with no-op actions and mutex (mutual exclusion) pairs; once the goals appear together without being mutex, search backwards through the graph for a plan, memoising failed goal sets.
- [Partial Order Planning](https://1mystic.github.io/SearchStudio/learn/plan-pop.html): Search in the space of partial plans. Start with steps Start (effects = initial state) and Finish (preconditions = goal). Repeatedly pick an open precondition, support it with an existing or a new step via a causal link, and resolve threats by promotion or demotion. Backtrack when stuck.
- [Means-ends analysis](https://1mystic.github.io/SearchStudio/learn/plan-mea.html): Compare the current state with the goal, pick the most important difference, look up an operator that removes it in the difference table, and recursively make that operator's preconditions true first. No protection of earlier achievements, so interacting goals (Sussman) defeat it.
- [Multi-arm plan scheduling (makespan)](https://1mystic.github.io/SearchStudio/learn/plan-multi-arm.html): Take a sequential plan from forward, backward or goal-stack planning and run it on k arms at once. Two moves may overlap only if they touch different blocks; moves that share a block keep their order. The number of time steps is the makespan.

## Week 9

- [AO*](https://1mystic.github.io/SearchStudio/learn/andor-ao-star.html): Follow the marked (currently best) connectors from the start to an unexpanded node, expand it, then revise costs upwards: each node's cost is its cheapest connector, an AND connector costs the sum over its children. A node is solved when all children of its marked connector are solved.
- [Backward chaining (goal tree)](https://1mystic.github.io/SearchStudio/learn/rules-backward-chaining.html): Goal-directed reasoning over a rule base: to prove a goal, either find it among the facts or find a rule whose THEN part matches it and prove every IF condition of that rule as a sub-goal (AND). Different rules for the same goal are alternatives (OR). The search is drawn as an AND–OR goal tree.

## Week 10

- [Forward chaining](https://1mystic.github.io/SearchStudio/learn/rules-forward-chaining.html): Repeat the recognise–act cycle: match every rule against working memory to build the conflict set, choose one instantiation by a conflict-resolution strategy, fire it (add or remove facts), until no new instantiation remains.
- [Rete algorithm](https://1mystic.github.io/SearchStudio/learn/rules-rete.html): Compile the conditions into a network. Alpha nodes test one pattern and remember the facts that pass; beta (join) nodes combine partial matches with consistent variable bindings; terminal nodes feed the conflict set. A new fact only travels the paths it affects, so nothing is re-matched.

## Week 11

- [Backtracking](https://1mystic.github.io/SearchStudio/learn/csp-backtracking.html): Assign variables one at a time in a fixed order, trying values in order. If a value conflicts with an earlier assignment try the next; if none is left, go back to the previous variable (chronological backtracking).
- [Forward checking](https://1mystic.github.io/SearchStudio/learn/csp-forward-checking.html): Combine search and reasoning: after assigning a variable, delete the values of its future neighbours that conflict with it. If some future domain becomes empty, backtrack at once instead of discovering the failure later.
- [Arc consistency (AC-1, AC-3)](https://1mystic.github.io/SearchStudio/learn/csp-ac3.html): Delete every value that has no supporting value in a neighbouring variable. Revise(X, Y) removes unsupported values of X with respect to Y. AC-1 sweeps all arcs until nothing changes; AC-3 keeps a queue and re-examines only the arcs into a variable whose domain shrank.
- [Matching diagram and arc consistency](https://1mystic.github.io/SearchStudio/learn/csp-matching-diagram.html): Draw each variable's domain as a column of dots and join two dots by a line when the pair is allowed by a binary constraint. Then run arc consistency on the picture: a dot with no line towards a neighbouring column has no support and is deleted, which may orphan dots in other columns.
- [Path consistency (PC, i-consistency)](https://1mystic.github.io/SearchStudio/learn/csp-path-consistency.html): Go beyond arc consistency: for every triangle X, Z, Y keep a pair (a, b) in the relation R(X,Y) only if some value c of Z is compatible with both (a, c) in R(X,Z) and (c, b) in R(Z,Y). This tightens the constraints themselves (it can empty a relation) and finds failures that arc consistency cannot see.
- [Waltz algorithm](https://1mystic.github.io/SearchStudio/learn/csp-waltz.html): Interpret a line drawing of a polyhedral scene. Each junction starts with every labelling its type allows (L, fork, arrow, T); a labelling survives only if each of its lines can get the same label from the junction at the other end. Propagate with an AC-3 style queue.
- [Strong k-consistency check (k ≤ 3)](https://1mystic.github.io/SearchStudio/learn/csp-k-consistency.html): Test i-consistency directly from the definition for i = 1, 2, 3: every consistent assignment to i − 1 variables must extend to any i-th variable. Each failing assignment is shown with what it implies: a value to delete (i = 2, arc consistency) or a forbidden pair, an induced nogood (i = 3, path consistency).
- [Model-based diagnosis](https://1mystic.github.io/SearchStudio/learn/csp-diagnosis.html): Assume components work as their models say and propagate values through the circuit. A contradiction with an observation implicates the components whose models were used: a conflict set. A diagnosis is a minimal set of components that hits every conflict.
- [SAT as a CSP: backtracking with unit propagation (DPLL)](https://1mystic.github.io/SearchStudio/learn/sat-dpll.html): Treat each variable as a CSP variable with domain {T, F} and each clause as a constraint. Backtracking assigns variables one at a time; unit propagation (a clause with one open literal forces it) and pure literals prune the tree, and an empty clause forces a backtrack. It is complete: it can also prove a formula unsatisfiable.

## Week 12

- [Partial look-ahead](https://1mystic.github.io/SearchStudio/learn/csp-lookahead-partial.html): Forward checking plus one directed pass over the future variables: every future variable is revised against the future variables that come after it in the ordering. Cheaper than full look-ahead, catches fewer dead ends.
- [Full look-ahead](https://1mystic.github.io/SearchStudio/learn/csp-lookahead-full.html): Forward checking plus one pass of arc revision over every arc between future variables (both directions). Detects dead ends that forward checking cannot, e.g. a future variable squeezed empty by two other future variables.
- [Arc-consistency look-ahead (MAC)](https://1mystic.github.io/SearchStudio/learn/csp-lookahead-mac.html): After each assignment, restore full arc consistency among the future variables with AC-3 (MAC: maintaining arc consistency). The strongest of the three look-aheads and the one with the smallest search tree.
- [Conflict-directed backjumping](https://1mystic.github.io/SearchStudio/learn/csp-cbj.html): Backtracking that remembers WHY each variable failed. Every variable keeps a conflict set (the earlier variables whose values ruled out its values). When a variable runs out of values, jump straight back to the deepest variable in its conflict set instead of the previous one, skipping variables that played no part in the failure.
- [Depth-First Branch and Bound](https://1mystic.github.io/SearchStudio/learn/search-dfbnb.html): Depth-first search that remembers the best solution cost U found so far and abandons any path whose g + h is already ≥ U. Linear memory, and optimal when h is admissible.
- [Nogood recording](https://1mystic.github.io/SearchStudio/learn/csp-nogood.html): Backtracking that learns. When a variable runs out of values, the assignments in its conflict set cannot be extended to a solution: store them as a nogood. Before trying any later value, check whether the assignment would contain a stored nogood and, if so, reject it without searching.

- [Full text of every explanation](https://1mystic.github.io/SearchStudio/llms-full.txt)
